Assignment 02 / Sculpting for Design

Memories in Miniature

Paper boats, school mornings, and a bird with binoculars: I turned a few childhood memories into small clay forms.

Memory · Sketching · Clay

I explored several childhood memories through sketches before choosing a familiar lunchbox and a coppersmith barbet as subjects for my sculptures.

01

Before the clay, a memory

One of my early sketches returns to rainy days with my brother. We would make paper boats, put them into streams of rainwater along the road, and run beside them as they sailed away. I wanted to record the shared activity as well as the objects themselves.

I also sketched school lunches and dance classes. I used stacked steel dabbas through much of my schooling. When my mother packed the same lunchbox again during an internship in my home city, it brought those memories back. My childhood weekends were also closely connected with Mohiniyattam classes.

02

School mornings, in miniature

I made the stacked lunchbox alongside a dosa tawa. Together, they recall two parts of my school mornings: breakfast at home and the lunch I carried to school.

I used to eat dosa with chutney powder while watching Oggy and the Cockroaches before school. Modelling these familiar objects gave me a way to make that routine tangible.

03

Listening for the coppersmith

My brother introduced my family to birdwatching. Many of our trips have revolved around it, and the coppersmith barbet is a bird I associate with those shared experiences.

Its call sounds like a metalworker striking copper. Whenever we heard it, my brother and I would compete to see who could spot the bird first. I explored its shape through drawings before making the sculpture.

04

A bird that watches birds

I added binoculars around the barbet’s neck as a reminder of the hours we spent birdwatching as children. That small detail connects the bird with the people looking for it.

I photographed the sculpture from different angles to show its beak, rounded head, tail, and incised surface marks. The binoculars give the familiar bird a personal connection to my memory.

05

What the objects remember

My two subjects hold different kinds of memory: the daily rhythm of breakfast and school, and the longer hours spent outdoors with my family. I used specific, ordinary details to give those recollections a physical form.

I kept the sketches as part of the project because they record the memories I considered along the way, including the ones I did not turn into finished sculptures.
